utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning everyone. I understand there's a change in the witness schedule. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone. Yesterday evening at the last proofing we obtained information according to which the very important documents that we haven't had access to so far - we weren't even aware of them - and they're extremely important for the Defence. All we are requesting is that the order of witnesses be changed so we can tender these documents and show these documents, because there's no other way to do it. We can't do it through anyone else, because the witness himself produced these documents. We need this witness, therefore, to return so that we can deal with those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's difficult for me to understand is the fact that witness has three or four binders of material relevant to your case has come to light only on the date before testimony. Does it not reveal that the Defence team does not really know what the witness will testify about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, had I been in the field I would have known how to look for every document that he has mentioned, but the investigator is there on his own and he doesn't have any direct contact, any sure contact with me. It couldn't have been otherwise. No one from the Prosecution was in the detention unit when preparing the course, but when we are preparing the Defence, without me, and it is I who am well-versed in all the various elements, it's not possible to do everything properly. These documents confirm what he will be testifying about. We know what he'll be testifying about, but these documents confirm that, and they confirm the Defence's positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you have any observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I spoke briefly with the Defence about this. I mean, I am aware of the fact that exigencies arise during the course of the case. Nevertheless, normally speaking, lapses in investigations are taken into account, and if they belatedly arise, then parties live with that. I was much more concerned about the impact of this proposed scheduling change on the Prosecution's ability to prepare for the following witnesses, so I tended to focus on that. I mentioned to the Defence that I consider that the reason they presented to us by e-mail last night for the proposed rescheduling of this witness might well be one that would cause the Court concern, and I didn't go farther than that with them. It's not clear to me. I don't know if the documents in fact are here and can be reviewed forthwith this week. I don't -- it's not clear to me why they can't be obtained immediately and reviewed quickly for that purpose. Beyond that, I wanted to emphasise that the repeated adjustments to the schedule have wreaked havoc on the Prosecution's ability to prepare, have caused us endless amounts of unnecessary work and considerable stress. This was another example of that. At the same time, the Defence has been extremely accommodating when we've requested adjustments based on the new state of play. So it does appear that there's a considerable degree of disorganisation, that it has an adverse impact on the Prosecution and will have -- I think will have an adverse impact this week requiring some adjustments to the schedule at the moment if, in fact, Mr. Skiljevic is not going to testify this week, but I -- it would be unfair if I didn't acknowledge the fact that within those -- that level of disorganisation the Defence has tried to ameliorate some of the -- some of the adverse impact to the extent they could by consulting with the Prosecution. So I -- this is what I have to leave to the Court: I simply don't understand the circumstances that gave rise to this emergency request for rescheduling sufficiently, but I can only note that no investigation can ever be considered to be complete. They can always go on and on and on, and that's a factor that both parties have to live with during the course of the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, I would like to remind everyone of the fact that it's not only that we started earlier than we wanted to in March, but in less than two months we called 50 witnesses, and it is not that easy to follow such a pace. There were 50 witnesses, because the Prosecution in fact is using a little less time on its cross-examination. So believe me, this is not deliberate. There are no shortcomings when it comes to the Defence's organisation. It's just that the pace is very brisk. Could this be taken into consideration, because we have called so many witnesses in less than two months, and by the break we will have had 50 plus 5 or 6 pursuant to 92 ter. So the number of witnesses is quite enormous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I do believe that all the parties are doing their best, and it's a fact that we are -- the speed we are proceeding is something unanticipated before. But in any event, my point is that there are still points on the part of the Defence to improve in terms of organisation or preparation. It's difficult to understand that those material you refer to could not have been found without your involvement. Well, that said, unless there's anything further we'll bring in the next witness. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. I also broached this with Mr. Sladojevic briefly. It's not entirely clear to me why we couldn't proceed with the witness and then he could be recalled if necessary to elaborate on any additional documentation that might be considered significant by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you assist us on this point, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There three or four binders containing additional documents, but I thought you had already decided about the next witness, so I didn't want to get involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I take it your next witness is Mr. Izo Golic. Very well. Let's bring him in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't quite -- I mean, I'm not sure what the point is here. I don't know what Mr. Karadzic means by you had already decided. I mean, we were notified last night -- this -- that that was the Defence's intention. Now I'm simply wondering if this option has been considered and -- and if not, why not, and the -- I don't understand what Dr. Karadzic means by three or four binders that he didn't want to get involved with. Again, part of the reason why I was not in a position to opine more directly on what steps could be taken -- I don't know if that means the binders are here and they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- declined to look at them or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If a party's not minded to present a specific witness, is the Chamber still entitled to oblige the party to present specific witness? Is that your case, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wasn't asking you to order the Defence to do so under these circumstances, but it did seem to me that the Court was trying from the outset to grapple with the question of what happened, why and what the options were, and that seemed to me to be one option that was at least worth considering. It doesn't seem to have been reviewed by the Defence, and Dr. Karadzic's response to the Court's inquiry about that didn't illuminate it, but, no, I'm not asking you to order the Defence to do so at this point, although -- although I do think that there are circumstances where the Court could invoke its inherent power to regulate the proceedings by saying the witness must go forward or not be called at all, but I'm not asking the Court here to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. And I take it you have no problem to proceed with this witness at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We have no -- I -- one of the reasons I wanted to discuss the entirety of the scheduling -- actually, we can proceed with this witness, but then when the witness leaves the stand, I think we have to discuss the remainder of the week's schedule because that is a problem in light of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So we don't need to stop now, but it's when this witness is completed I think we need to get some strong clarity on the remainder of the week, and we have a lot of flexibility as the Court knows in terms of time, but we will need to adapt some significant adjustments so the Prosecution is in a position to [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was your microphone on?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Was it off? I'm so sorry. I might have turned it off prematurely. Anyway, I do want to speak with the Court about how to proceed after this witness, but the good news, to the extent it exists, is that we -- we have sufficient time this week to make appropriate adjustments that will allow the Prosecution to proceed under these circumstances, assuming that we modify the schedule accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. After we have heard Mr. Golic's evidence, we'll have some more concrete words as to the scheduling for the remainder of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Golic, I apologise for your inconvenience. Would you take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Golic.

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give the Defence a statement?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The statement will be in the e-court system in a minute or two. I'd like to see 1D6720. Have you read this statement?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you to make a break between question and answer, and I'll have to remind myself of that as well so that it's easier for the interpreters. Is everything you said accurately reflected in that statement?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't know if it's only my e-court, because I believe the witness is answering these questions without being able to see his statement, because we don't have his statement displayed on our screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will appear any minute now. We sent it digitally, but we don't have the same means as the Prosecution, so our Case Manager can't upload it directly. It has to go through an intermediary from the Registry, and therefore we depend on the Registry for this, but it was sent on Saturday, and we complete the statements after the proofing when the witness signs it, and that's what they do, too, but they can upload it directly. We can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does it mean that there's no revision from the draft statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it's necessary to review, revise -- well, it wasn't signed up to the proofing, after the last proofing. When the witness confirms that there are no mistakes, that everything is accurate, then it is signed, we sent it, but we can't upload it. And I don't see why our Case Manager shouldn't be in a position to upload it as well, but this is identical to the draft version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. My question was not precise. My point was whether there's any change from the draft version, and I take it the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Golic, do you have your statement with you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And on that basis are you satisfied with proceeding at the moment, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sure. I think we could also probably upload the draft, which I thought was 1D6301, and then we can all see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. 1D6301.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Golic, can you see your statement on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You signed the statement, and it accurately reflects what you said; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would the gist of your answers be the same as the answers you provided in the statement?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, they should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Golic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender the statement. 1D6720 is the number. It will be in the e-court system very soon. We don't have any associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection to the admission of the signed statement which is to be uploaded --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- in due course. We'll give the number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6720 receives number D2665, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would now like to read out a brief summary of the testimony. [In English] Lieutenant Izo Golic did his compulsory military service in Subotica in 1984 on 12-millimetre mortars and was discharged from the JNA with the rank of lance corporal, trained for the duties of commander of the 120-millimetre mortar squad. While in the army, he was awarded the highest military commendation. He was assigned to the 120-millimetre Mortar Battery of the 216th Mountain Brigade of the JNA. Later, the brigade was renamed 1st Romanija Brigade, Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Lieutenant Golic was aware that the Muslims were arming themselves before the war. In early 1991, he bought a car from a Muslim company, however, he never received the car. When he and a member of other customers who had not received their cars visited the flat of one of the company's owners, a large number of weapons were found in the flat. In June 1991, following the events in Slovenia and Croatia, there was a general mobilisation of the 216th Mountain Brigade which recently after that went to Banja Luka. However, due to an insufficient turnout of the reserve forces, mainly because Muslim soldiers did not respond to the call-up, the command was forced to reassign soldiers who had not necessarily completed the appropriate training. Whilst the brigade was in Banja Luka, two buses of the reservist soldiers' relatives visited the unit and encouraged them to go home as the Muslim soldiers had returned home or not responded to the mobilisation and many Serb villages were unprotected. Following this, soldiers began leaving en masse until the command had to return the unit to base due to the lack of soldiers. Izo Golic thought the political situation had calmed down. However, the killing of a Serb wedding guest in March 1992 resulted in fear and anxiety amongst the Serbian people. The Serbian people began to organise themselves and a meeting was organised in the village of Gucevo for those people who were in favour of preserving Yugoslavia. Mainly Serbs attended. On 16th of March, 1992, Izo Golic was called up for training. The soldiers were given basic training. The reason for this training was that a large percentage of the brigade were Muslim soldiers who had left the JNA. Therefore, the brigade was replenished and the soldiers required training. In April 1992, the 216th Mountain Brigade was given orders to remove the JNA weapons and military equipment from the depot in Faletici. On 2nd of May, Muslim forces carried out an all-out attack on the JNA in Sarajevo and the Rogatica battalion was mobilised. Attack was repeated on 3rd of May. Approximately half of the soldiers did not come as they feared for their lives or the lives of their families. Once the battalion arrived in their positions, they -- in Sarajevo region, they were under constant sniper fire from the Muslim forces from Mojmilo. The battery was never manned to full capacity, and many of the soldiers had not undergone any training for the battery. The soldiers received orders regarding which targets to hit from higher commands, and they mainly fired at previously spotted enemy targets from which they were being fired at, and the battery would target staging areas of the enemy infantry forces, several of which were civilian facilities. On numerous occasions the Muslim forces would fire from the Kosevo Hospital complex, always during cease-fires. However, the Serb forces never received an order to return fire on the complex. On one occasion the Serbian forces could not discern the weapons being used to fire upon them from the national museum, and although they wished to return fire, they received orders prohibiting operations against such facilities. Muslim forces used the Jewish Cemetery near Grbavica to attack, using tombstones as cover. The Serbian forces did not enter the cemetery. The Muslim forces had 120-millimetre mortars mounted on the vans or trucks and tanks. Muslim forces would fire at the Serbian forces and then retreat into a tunnel. They also had mortars mounted on the freight cars on the railway that would fire shells toward the Serbian positions. The Serbian forces only returned fire when they were being targeted by the Muslim forces. The Muslim forces -- the Muslims were able to gain heavy artillery weapons by seizing army barracks in Sarajevo, primarily the Marsal Tito Barracks. The Muslim forces attempted to seize the positions of the Serbian forces nearly every day. His unit had strict orders not to open fire without authorisation and operations against civilians were prohibited. The soldiers were ordered to respect the Geneva Conventions. A letter from the command was circulated amongst the soldiers. The letter stated that any soldier who disobeyed this would face punishment. Izo Golic's battery never fired shells for the purpose of intentionally -- intentionally hitting civilians. They opened fire only on military targets. The targets at which they fired were usually decided in advance on the basis of information received from their men at positions. Izo Golic does not think that there were any civilians on the lines of disengagement. His unit evacuated civilians from their front lines. The roads and streets of Grbavica were constantly exposed to the Muslim sniper fire, and so shields were erected to hide civilians from the view of Muslim snipers. The Lukavica-Vrace-Trebevic-Pale road was constantly under sniper fire, so the Serbs were forced to use a much longer road of inferior quality. This means -- this meant that the transportation of wounded became very long and labourious as the road was still not safe and also came under fire from snipers. The snipers were positioned at the top of exclusively civilian buildings and fire was opened almost constantly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have Mr. Golic's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I wouldn't normally by any means rise at this point, but I find myself compelled to ask for a citation for something Dr. Karadzic has read in the summary which I'm presently not able find in the witness's evidence, and that line -- what he's read that I question appears at page 11, lines 13 and 14, the sentence saying: "Attack was repeated on 3 May -- on 3rd of May." The immediately preceding sentence which Dr. Karadzic read out is contained in paragraph 12 of the witness's statement, but I simply don't find this sentence I've just referred to anywhere in the witness's evidence. I may be wrong, in which case I would be quite happy to hear that, but otherwise I wonder if I could have a citation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Bearing the caveat that the summary does not form the part of the evidence in any means, but could you clarify, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this comes from me. It's not in the statement. But I think that this is such a well-known thing that happened. It was even more drastic on the 3rd of May, and that's why I thought that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's unacceptable. It's not you that is giving evidence, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but as I said, since this is not evidence, I mean, the summary not evidence, I just thought that it should be made clear to you which attack this is about, but in the future I shall strictly adhere to the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point in time I have no more questions for corporal Golic. The statement is already in e-court. 1D6720 is the name -- is the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Golic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in Mr. Karadzic's Defence case has been admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, Ms. Edgerton. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Golic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Good morning. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Golic, just before we begin, can you confirm that this isn't the first time you've testified before this Tribunal? You also appeared as a Defence witness in the prosecution of General Galic in 2002.

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: That's right, madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And can you also confirm that you served in the immediate Sarajevo theatre only up until October 1992? After that, you returned to Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when we look at your statement, we should understand a number of the paragraphs, 13, 16, 17, 18, 21, 22, 23, 24, 26, 27, and 28, all your observations set out in those paragraphs are limited to that time period, up until October 1992?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your unit never returned to the Sarajevo theatre any time after that; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: The unit no longer existed when we returned to Rogatica. It was attached to Light Rogatica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The interpreter just did not hear your very last sentence after the words, "It was attached to the Light Rogatica Brigade." Could you repeat that and probably speak a bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: All right. We no longer returned to the Sarajevo theatre.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. Now, in your statement, at paragraph 31 you said, "... every target" --

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: May I? I don't have the statement here. May I put it -- here it says no page currently available. I don't have it on the screen, so it's not available. Can I take out the statement, my own copy? Can I use a hard copy of the statement, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Golic, by all means. No problem with you consulting your own statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you could go to paragraph 31 there you said: "... every target azimuth would be determined and any corrections were carried out during shooting. As far as 120-millimetre shells are concerned, a target is considered hit if the shell falls within a radius of 50 metres." So tell me if I have this right. That means if the first shell falls outside the 50-metre [Realtime transcript read in error "30-meter"] radius, then one would have to adjust the fire and fire again until the target is hit. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Fifty metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. The transcript presently reads "30," and that should be "50." You're correct. So do I understand your evidence correctly in paragraph 31 then, Mr. Golic?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that this is a term that is used in artillery and that is called guiding. First it was the 3rd unit, the 3rd squad that acted, and the rest can act only when the target is reached.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, another question about targeting. To effectively neutralise a military target, any kind of structure or building, for example, you'd never fire just one mortar round, would you?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: It all depends on the effects attained. Sometimes only one can destroy a target, say if it's a question of snipers. We were not destroying a facility. We were neutralising enemy personnel.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you needed to neutralise a facility, would you do that by firing only one round?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Again, I'm telling you if the effect has been achieved, then one shell is sufficient. If we had set targets, places where the enemy soldiers gathered, the enemy soldiers that were firing at our positions, then we had the possibility of having these set targets as they're known in artillery-speak; that is to say they had been located earlier on and determined earlier on. That's what I'm saying in my statement too. I don't see that there's anything different there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Uh-huh. So you would continue to fire until the target is neutralised. It depends on the effect, what you've been able to achieve.

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Well, in principle that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now, for targets like a facility or a building, it's correct that you would use a delayed-fuse mortar to fire, wouldn't you, in order to achieve the maximum effect?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: The delayed fuses were used.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. And just always on -- with an eye to adjustments you had to do while firing, I want to ask you about the type of ammunition you had at your disposal. Is it correct that while you were deployed in Sarajevo, you started to receive shells that were intended -- that had been repaired and with different gunpowder charges from older production which had been warehoused for a long time?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Seventeen kilogramme charges were used, contact-fuse shells mostly, but we could not determine whether that is what was according to standards. All charges are fairly similar. Of course with mortar batteries, it's always important to determine a number of elements, the altitude, the pressure, and so on, but of course there are people who have to do that. We had mathematics professors who were doing that for us and who did an excellent job.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So to go back to my question, I asked you whether it was correct that you started to receive shells that had been repaired and shells with different gunpowder charges of older production that had been warehoused for a long time, and is your answer to that yes or no?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: For older ones, no, but there were these overhauled mines -- or, rather, shells that were produced at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that would affect precision of the mortar shells, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Well, it would affect them, but all these factors had to be taken into account. So there is always a risk with the first shell that is fired. That is an inevitable thing as far as artillery is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 18 of your statement, you talk about tanks held by the ABiH across from your zone two tanks. Can you confirm that these two tanks, would could only -- or you could only see the barrels? You couldn't actually see the tanks, could you?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: The tanks' turrets could be seen as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the tanks -- the tanks were actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript, 23, 24, page 18, the witness said that all of that was taken into account by the persons who were doing the calculations, all of these elements that would change the status of the shells. So the word "the persons who would be doing the calculations" is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Golic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you can confirm, can't you, that these tanks of which you could only see the turrets were actually dug in, they were immobile; correct?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you didn't personally see them firing either, did you, you personally?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: No. Perhaps they were mobile. When I saw them, they were dug in below Kosevsko Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have anything further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Golic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps Dr. Karadzic might have a question in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. I take it -- Mr. Golic, I apologise. I was carried away to hectic witness schedule order. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellencies, just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could I ask you, Lieutenant, on which occasions was only one or shells -- one or two shells fired? Can you remind us when it was sufficient to fire only one or two shells?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly when it had to do with sniper shooters who would stop shooting immediately or other targets that were not there when the enemy attack was being prepared, so that is to say that if there was individual firing at our lines. Perhaps it was not explained here that we had two companies in the battalion that were located at the Jewish Cemetery and next to Vrbanja Bridge, and our units were most often fired at at the Jewish Cemetery. So the enemy forces if they would fire at us up there, then we would respond with one or two shells but only on orders. I point that out once again here. It was strictly forbidden to wilfully target without orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you conclude on the basis of the number of shells, if there was just one or two shells, whether it would happen that one or two shells would be fired with a view to terrorising civilians in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: Civilians were never our target, and we never thought --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not necessary. Mr. Karadzic, that's typical leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the Presiding Judge, if I may, could I just say two words? This question is a question that is being brought up time and time again in the media in the federation. When I arrived here, I was assaulted verbally by a newspaper, and I'm probably going to sue them. It's on account on what President Karadzic asked me about now, and I think that that has to do with that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's unnecessary this time, Mr. Golic. If you could concentrate on answering the question posed by Mr. Karadzic. It is Mr. Karadzic to pose questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Excellencies, this was based on the question put by the learned Ms. Edgerton, one or two shells, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the question would then be: In these situations when you fired one or two shells, was your intention to terrorise the citizens of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: IZO GOLIC
utterances.text: That was not our intention, and I think that citizens were not at the lines between the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. No normal person would keep their civilian population on the lines themselves. I believe that they had been moved elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Lieutenant Golic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That really concludes your evidence, Mr. Golic. On behalf the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You're free to go now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, and I wish you success in your work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Come back to the scheduling -- witness scheduling issue. So could you help me, Mr. Karadzic, as regards Mr. -- what's the name? Mr. Skiljevic. I understand he's here at The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Last night we had a proofing session with Mr. Skiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you do not have his material you referred to in your possession yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We just received information to the effect that this kind of material does exist and it is his lawyer in Sarajevo who has that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, would there be any problem if we proceed with his evidence and then if need be you can recall him once you have received the -- all the documents and reviewed them?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, the entire course of the examination-in-chief will be different once we've had these documents made available to us, the entire course, if you will. The entire course of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you prepared a draft witness statement which you will not change, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was prepared in the stage when we were not aware of the existence of these documents. That's the problem. The main Defence counsel is in detention, and that's the problem, whereas that is not the case with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, what's the remainder of the witness schedule for this week be like? So next we'll hear who?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maksimovic would be next now, and then these five witness -- these five witnesses and the six the one, Mr. Golic. That would be all the witnesses for this week. So Maksimovic -- this would be the order: Maksimovic, Salipur, Stanic, Sojic, Vujasin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And any observation or problem on the part of the Prosecution, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you -- thank you, Mr. President. Yes, there is. First of all, with respect to the very next witness, I believe that -- who will be taken by Ms. Edgerton, I believe there's some logistical issues that need to be resolved. We had to adjust for the purposes of uploading documents, and in addition, she anticipated at least a little more time, but more importantly with respect to the other three -- four witnesses, rather, Mr. Vujasin in fixed for Thursday. So let's set him aside. With respect to Salipur, Stanic and Sojic, given our efforts and timing, we would simply ask that their examinations in chief be handled today and the cross-examinations be kicked over to tomorrow. That seems to me to be at least a modestly fair request under the circumstances. It won't cost us any time, particularly given the fact that Mr. Vujasin won't be testifying until Thursday and we will obviously complete the examination of these witnesses with ample remaining time this week. So that's simply it. We need a little break. I need to consult Ms. Edgerton for how long before Mr. Maksimovic. Then we could proceed to do Mr. Salipur, Stanic and Sojic in chief today, conduct their cross-examinations tomorrow and conclude with Mr. Vujasin on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the crux of your submission is that we would not enter into cross-examination of any of those three witnesses, Salipur, Stanic and Sojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you take any position with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That isn't a problem for the Defence. That isn't a problem for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then before bringing the next witness, the Chamber will now issue an oral ruling on the Prosecution's motion to exclude in part the evidence of Witness Zdravko Salipur filed on the 12th of December, 2012, wherein the Prosecution requests that the Chamber order that part of paragraph 24 as well as paragraphs 25 to 28 be excluded from the witness statement. The Prosecution submits that these paragraphs are irrelevant to the charges in the indictment as they pertain to crimes allegedly committed by Muslims against Serb citizens of Sarajevo in Popalic in May 1992. I said Popalic. The accused responded on 13th of December, 2012, opposing the motion and submitting that the expected evidence is relevant to rebut the allegations in paragraph 14(C) to the indictment that the accused was "disseminating, encouraging, and/or facilitating the dissemination of propaganda to Bosnian Serbs." The accused further contends that the expected testimony is relevant to show that crimes alleged in the indictment may have been committed out -- committed out of revenge and to provide context to the events in Sarajevo in 1992. The Chamber considers that the information in part of paragraph 24 as well as paragraphs 25 to 28, which is sought for exclusion, is no different from the information which in the Chamber's practice has been excluded on the ground that it is detailed tu quoque evidence. The Chamber therefore grants the motion and excludes paragraph 24 from "on the 4th of May, 1992," onwards as well as paragraphs 25 to 28 and allows the accused to tender the remainder of Zdravko Salipur's statement pursuant to Rule 92 ter. Finally, the Chamber orders that the Prosecution shall have about an hour for its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to -- Mr. President, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to remind the Court. We can proceed with the examination-in-chief. Ms. Edgerton, as I mentioned, had some issues both technical in nature and otherwise that needed to be resolved before she could commence cross. She can do it today, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take break after the examination-in-chief and see where we are afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksimovic. Please make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Colonel, or would it be better to say Naval Captain.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give the Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since we are speaking the Serbian language, I would like to ask you to make a pause for the benefit of the interpreters and the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D6709 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see the -- can you see the statement on the screen?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you read the statement? Have you signed it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please just wait for the transcript to come to an end. Does this statement accurately reflect what you said?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, the same questions that were put to you by the Defence team, would your answers in substance be same time?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now read out a brief summary in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I tender this statement now? We also have four associated documents. There are no additional ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll give the numbers for both versions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6709 receives number D2666. Associated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are dealing with the 92 ter statement only. So we -- D2666 will be admitted and put under seal, and public -- we give the public redacted version number of Defence Exhibit D2667. And let's come to the issues of associated exhibit. Do you have any observations, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I do, actually. I -- my submission would be -- pardon me one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you are tendering four documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I -- my submission would be the document in paragraph 71. 1D8357 is not -- actually it's irrelevant and the same with respect to 1D8356, 1D8357 being not by the nature of their comments an indispensable part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's deal with the associated exhibits one by one. Shall we upload first 1D8110. My question is whether the English translation is a correct one. I see three pages in the B/C/S version and the English seems to be only one page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's possible, your Excellency. It was used in the course of the previous testimony, and we were satisfied with what had been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the English translation is the translation of part of the document referring to para 1 only, "Enemy."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you're right. Perhaps it should be marked for identification because on the next page -- or, rather, on the last page there is a paragraph which is about the relationship between these two high-ranking officers and it could be of importance. It wasn't admitted in the course of the first testimony. Could we see the third page in the Serbian language. Or could we do this live.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a translation of this document. I can ask my colleague Ms. Langenberg, who by the way hasn't appeared before Your Honours yet in these proceedings, to release that, and that's going to be of assistance. And relying on the existing translation, Your Honours, I apologise, I didn't realise the one that had been uploaded was incomplete. My oversight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then we'll admit this one as an associated exhibit. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be D2668, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Karadzic, in coming to 1D8357, I agree with Ms. Edgerton that it's irrelevant. So if you have specific points, I would like you to lead live with the witness. And with respect to other documents referred to by Ms. Edgerton, the Chamber is of the view that it forms indispensable and inseparable part of the document, so we'll admit them too, the two documents. Shall we give the numbers for 8356 and 8358.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 8356 receives number D2669 and document 8358 receives number D2670, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellencies. Ideal with that document after I have read out the summary. I will now read out the summary in English. [In English] Ratomir Maksimovic was born on 13th of February, 1993 -- 1943. Between 12th of November, 1990 and June 1991, he was employed at the JNA school centre, Banjica, department of naval tactics. Between June 1991 and 22nd of April, 1992, he worked at the military historical institute, Belgrade. Ratomir Maksimovic was transferred as -- at personal request from Belgrade to the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo because he is originally from Ilidza and his family was there at the time. Between April 22nd, 1992, and June the 22nd, 1992, he worked at Sarajevo at the 2nd Military District as an information organ. Between June the 2nd -- 22nd, 1992, and April the 1st, 1993, he returned to work at the military historical institute in Belgrade. From April the 1st, 1993, to September the 1st, 1994, he was in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command. Between 1st of September, 1994, and 15th of October, 1994, he was assistant commander of the navy in Kumbor Montenegro in Yugoslav Army. Between 15th of October, 1994, and 30th of April, 1995, he worked in the history department of the military academy. Finally, between 30th of April, 1995, and 31st of March, 1996, he was once again in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Colonel Maksimovic has knowledge of the military organisation and arming of Muslims before the conflict broke out in -- in BH and Sarajevo. In Sarajevo city, the Muslim authorities had the 1st Corps of BH Army under their control between April 1992 and December 1995. They had positions at dominant high points in and around the city, including in civilians -- including in civilian features and heavy artillery spread out everywhere in the city. Its units also stretched deep in the area under Muslim control. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was a defence unit, and its members were aged from 20 to 60. In the entire Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, there were 20 -- 15 to 20 professional soldiers, most of them -- [indiscernible] most of them at command level. The rest were reserve officers and people trained on the job. It was mainly a people's army. The lack of professional command affected combat abilities of the units, which were not able to carry out offensive combat operations. Operations were not part of a systematic or widespread attack on civilians. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps could not and did not consciously make it impossible for the Muslim government in Sarajevo to control the conditions of life of the civilians in the city which they controlled. He did not -- Muslims controlled. He did not know that the final goal of the Serbian authorities was to divide Sarajevo. He did have knowledge about offers to completely demilitarise the city, which was personally advocated by Mr. Karadzic, as well as to surrendering control of the airport to the UN in June 1992 in an attempt to calm the war down. He also had knowledge of offers to have all heavy weapons of both sides placed under UN control, but there was a lot of mistrust on both sides regarding objective control by the international forces. There was no strategy. Instead, the situation was imposed by the 1st Corps of BH Army and not by Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Had the 1st Corps of BH Army broken out of Sarajevo, it would have an affected the other fronts and the course of the war in BH. The main task was to protect Serbian territories and the civilian population and to prevent any mass movement of the BH Army 1st Corps in Sarajevsko Polje. This prevented these forces from joining others and massacre civilian positions and -- Serbian positions and civilians. He draws this conclusion based on the fact that when he was captured by the Muslim paramilitary forces and held at Hotel Evropa, he was told that after breaking through to Ilidza, Muslim forces would kill and slaughter anyone in their way. They had no intention -- the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had no intention of causing civilian casualties or terrorising or having psychological impact on the civilians in the area under Muslim control. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps did not issue or receive any oral or written orders to attack civilians or means of public transportation in the area of the city under Muslim control. General orders stated that fire should be opened against the positions from which it came and against moving forces intended for reinforcement. Political and military leadership from the beginning of the war on the Serb side gave orders not to attack civilians. When military targets in civilian zones were attacked, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command warned the enemy by lodging protests with the UN. Whenever the command found out about possible civilian casualties, it suspended fire in order to avoid such victims. Conversely, civilians in the zone of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps were in a state of fear and uncertainty due to permanent shelling and sniping by the BH Army. Thousands of civilians were killed from the beginning of the war until the autumn 1995. Ammunition in Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was scarce and orders stated that it should be used as a rarely as possible. He had no knowledge of professional snipers in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps but knew about snipers in the BH Army 1st Corps and their firing against civilians in the city under Serbian control. There was also discussions about them firing also at civilians in the city under BH control, army -- BH Army control. The attitude of superior commands of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was that humanitarian aid should be supplied across Serbian territory. They had information about humanitarian convoys being misused by military -- for military purposes for the BH Army 1st Corps. UNPROFOR itself transported military materiel in these convoys. Therefore, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps occasionally checked convoys. They also had knowledge about the existence of a black market where those goods were sold in the city controlled by the Muslim authorities. As for civilian use of water, electricity and gas in the city under Muslim control, everything was normal during cease-fires. During combat, combat operations, supply was reduced but not because the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps but due to the operations from the city under Muslim control against power transmission lines and water supply system. Corps command of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps did not prevent the freedom of movement of civilians from one side to the other. They had knowledge that Serbian civilians in the part of the city under Muslim control were not allowed to leave the city. Security organs had information about the existence of criminal groups in the units of the BH Army 1st Corps, the activities of which would not have been possible without the approval of Alija Izetbegovic. Ratomir Maksimovic knew about the existence and production of modified air-bombs for defensive reasons to shoot at targets on the ground. They were in the arsenal of Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. They were used as a last resort and had a low range of 1 to 2 kilometres. In March 1994, a group of unarmed volunteers joined the Vogosca brigade to man positions of Golo Brdo and Vis. They stayed for less than a month and left unarmed. They were under the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command and adhered to the international law of war. The army was energetic to eliminate paramilitary formations whereas Muslim paramilitaries launched attacks on the JNA members. There was some friction and misunderstanding with municipal authorities in Vogosca regarding resources and attempts by civilian authorities to be involved in command and control. Mr. Maksimovic has no knowledge about the relationship between Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and general headquarter and the republican civilian authorities on the other side. I think it should be translated. No, it is corrected. In Serbian it was not corrected. [Interpretation] Could we see 1D8357, please, just to make sure of something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before doing that, you would not take long for the evidence in chief, but before doing that, when it comes to the statement of a military officer, I often find the Defence statement not complete in terms of position or ranks. So take a look at paragraph 5 of the witness statement, so third paragraph and last paragraph. The witness says: "Between 1st of April, 1993, and 1st of September 1994, I was at the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command." In what capacity and in what rank? And then last paragraph as well: "Between the 30th of April, 1995, and 31st May, 1996, I was once again in the SRK command." So could you lead the witness as to those points.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, did you understand these periods? Can you tell us what positions you held when you were first in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from the 1st of April, 1993, until the 1st of September, 1994?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since I come from the navy and that's rather special, I was chief for morale. Actually, I was assistant to Galic, so I was the number-two person in the department for morale and information.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the dates.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, as an officer from the corps I was sent to Vogosca, Blazuj, Ilidza several times, and I went there in the interests of the corps. I went to see how I could help them and so on and so forth. All right from April 1993 until the 1st of September, 1994, I was de jure and de facto chief for morale and information in the corps command. So I was subordinated to the assistant commander. Kosovac was Galic's assistant commander, whereas I was chief in that department. So I was the number two person for morale. However, since I came from the area myself, I was sent out to the area several times Hadzici, Blazuj, Ilidza to view the situation on the ground, and sometimes I'd stay there longer and I helped the officers in their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just slow down would you, please.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Has it been translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but please do slow down. So far they've done it.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: As far as 1995 is concerned -- or, rather, in September 1994 I left the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and I was in the navy. Well, you see, I was involved in teaching in military schools, but they asked me to go back to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps because General Milosevic had the intention of setting up barracks, barracks for Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and I would be in charge of organisation and establishing these barracks in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. So this is of just --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, can you not speak slowly. Could you please speak at a different pace altogether.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: All right. In 1995, in the month of April, at the request of General Milosevic, I came back to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps because General Milosevic wanted to establish barracks for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, that is to say to create a peacetime institution at the level of barracks. I was supposed to organise that and to establish this logistics institution for the army. However, in view of the situation in 1995, all the way up until -- well, throughout 1995, until Dayton, practically all that time was spent in combat operations because the corps was subjected to constant fighting all the way up to Dayton. In the meantime, our positions were bombed so I could not carry out this plan. I stayed with them until the 31st of March, 1996, when I asked in writing to be returned and General Milosevic allowed me to return to the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one more question. In the first period as chief of the organ for morale, you say that you toured different positions and reported on that. Who did you report to and about what?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly I report in writing and orally to Kosovac, my superior, and then he reports to Galic. So that's the chain. Kosovac was between us. He was my immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, will this do now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 1D8357, just for a moment, please. Could we please have that in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, Colonel, what this means: Officers at RKM Pale, and what does RKM mean?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: RKM is reserve or alternate command post. I was there from the 22nd until the 30th of April, 1992, at the Turist hotel. This was this hotel called Turist in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was the JNA at the moment?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the forward command post of the 2nd Military District.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can it be admitted now if it would assist the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why do we need this, Mr. Karadzic? I think we can do without it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, Excellency, but the JNA had all this organisation around Sarajevo, reserve command post, forward command post. I thought that this would complete the picture, if you will, of JNA action. The JNA was under threat. But I'm not opposing this. I mean, I don't mind not tendering this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, there's something missing here. We had a lieutenant-colonel or a Colonel Causevic, a Muslim, who was up there with us, and he seems to be missing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You're done, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a break for half an hour, but before that -- yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think Ms. Edgerton might have one matter to raise. I just wanted to note that I responded to the point about scheduling of the remaining four witnesses. I did not respond to Mr. Karadzic's point concerning the assertion that once he got the documents the entire course of examination-in-chief will be different. I think in fairness that's -- that seems a bit disingenuous. These are not documents related to an entirely new matter but documents apparently collected by and related to the witness who was relating his -- what he saw and experienced presumably to the Defence and that is reflected in his current statement. Beyond -- so beyond the fact that presumably the information in those documents --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tieger stop touching his microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry about that. That was already reflected in the statement, I think beyond that it would be rather speculative to suggest that for some reason all the information given by this witness is -- is going to change in the face of the documents which the witness had available to him the entire time. I think the most that can be said is there may or may not be documentary confirmation of what the witness is asserting in his statement. So I just wanted to make that observation in connection with the accused's remarks one way or the other. It wasn't clear to me whether the Court was still mulling over the schedule but I didn't have a chance to respond to that claim before. I think it is an accurate one and needed to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, do you wish to comment at all before --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only if the Chamber wants to review its decision. However, I must say if the Chamber is going to review the decision it has already reached, then I'm going to state my views. If not, there's no need for me to say anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we thank you very much indeed, but we see no reason to go back on our decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. Dr. -- Mr. Tieger behind me actually articulated my situation this morning, and I had actually -- knowing only the previous witness schedule, factored in a bit more time for my preparation to proceed with the cross-examination today, and I'd just like to ask you if I could be allowed to recover a little bit of that time and your indulgence for a break of longer than half an hour at this point, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long would you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I would ask for an hour. I would be prepared to go in whatever Your Honours determine, taking into account the rest of the schedule that we need to meet for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break for an hour and resume at quarter to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Maksimovic, as you have noted your evidence in chief was admitted in most part in written form in lieu of your oral testimony, now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Ms. Edgerton, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Maksimovic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Wonderful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to deal with a brief area in private session, if I may, and get it out of the way at the beginning of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you were also referred to, Mr. Maksimovic, by Mr. Seselj in his trial here at this Tribunal when at transcript page 8670 of those proceedings he put portions of a statement you gave in Belgrade to one of the witnesses in this Chamber, and my first question to you is: Can you confirm that as Mr. Seselj said in proceedings here, you gave a statement to his Defence team in the event you would be called as a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I know what I wrote. They wanted my opinion on the commanding officer of the combat line at the Jewish Cemetery, Aleksic, and I gave a statement to that Aleksic confirming that he was disciplined, that he worked in the corps, that he accomplished his missions and never committed any crimes. I just gave a positive opinion on Aleksic, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just with regard to the content of that statement, I'd like to read to you from page 8673 of the transcript in the Seselj proceedings something that Dr. -- or Mr. Seselj quoted, and I'd like to ask if you can confirm that. He says, starting at line 6 that you wrote: "Aleksic never undertook anything on his own initiative or without the knowledge of the corps command. He acted exclusively pursuant to orders." Can you confirm that that's what you set out in your statement for Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that, because that was also the opinion of the corps command, that he did not do anything. He just defended his very small area of responsibility very difficult and very dangerous, the Jewish Cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on to another area, and still for a moment on the subject of paramilitaries, the group of 40 unarmed men that you refer to in paragraph 57 of your statement, can you confirm that that was a group of Serbian Radical Party volunteers commanded by Vojvoda Jovo Ostojic? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the benefit of the witness, the Serbian interpretation was "Serbian Democratic Party," whereas the transcript is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The defence of Vogosca was a very difficult point for the corps command. Forty volunteers came, stayed for less than a month. They were not armed. I did not make any inquiries about them. I was apolitical. And they returned, and then later I learned that this Ostojic belonged to Seselj's party. I had no particular contact with them. I just saw them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So your answer to my question is yes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Jovo was a member of Seselj's party. That's what I learned. Now, who each of them individually was, I don't know. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this is the same group that had been participating in combat in Vogosca from the beginning of the war until the end of 1992 or the beginning of 1993, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. I was not present in Vogosca. I only arrived in 1993. What happened in 1992 in the autumn, I don't know, so I cannot say anything about that group. I don't know what they did. When I arrived, they were not there. More or less, all the paramilitaries were disbanded in 1992 or disarmed --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: -- because we were working on establishing military discipline. They were decimated, and they were no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I understand your answer, but if you could just focus on my questions. My next question is: This group when they arrived, as you said in March of 1993, were invited by the commander of the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade, Dragan Josipovic, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that he invited them. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to have a look, please, at 65 ter number --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's news to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 24073. It's a report of the VRS security organ dated 14 April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that, Mr. Maksimovic, you're familiar with who Colonel Ljubisa Beara is, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I know I've heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we go over to the next page of this document, please, in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, on this date Colonel Beara writes that he was at the Sarajevo 3rd Infantry Brigade intending a briefing of the battalion and assistant commanders and the briefing was led by Colonel Maksimovic, brigade Chief of Staff. The briefing was also attended by Vojvoda Jovo Ostojic, the commander of the SRS volunteers detachment which came to the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade at the end of March. So not only did you hear of him, you've actually met him on 12 April 1994, haven't you, Mr. Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I met him because he got a line to defend with those 40 men. He had to be present when tasks were issued, but that was not your original question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't deny that I met him. He led this group of 40 people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, the record does not reflect the answer of the question. It was not your question, he said, whether I met him or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I note that the very first paragraph of this document refers to you, Colonel Maksimovic, as Chief of Staff of the 3rd Sarajevo Infantry Brigade. You didn't mention that in your statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I said that the corps command sent me to Vogosca, to Ilidza and Hadzici to lend them assistance. I spent a very short time there until new people came to take over those duties, because I was not qualified, being from a different service of the army. I would be there for a transitional period of a month and a half. I said I've been to Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Maksimovic, you've actually previously said that you were ordered to report to Vogosca on 11 July 1993. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date, but I did go there certainly in different periods. On the 13th of July, yes, I went there.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that was to take up service with the Vogosca Tactical Group; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was at the staff of that group as the organ for morale, because a great Muslim offensive was going on in July in Vogosca. I was at the staff organising morale.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So when Colonel Beara reports on 12 April 1994 that you were Chief of Staff, are you saying that he's wrong in the report he made?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: In 1994, this Tactical Group was disbanded, and because staff was short, I was appointed Chief of Staff of the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade that was established at the time. So there was a tactical group that was disbanded to form the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade. I spent about a month and a half there before being taken back to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when Dr. Karadzic asked you about your military background, you didn't mention that to him either, your position as Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's not about my military background. I just carried out those duties. It's not part of my military career. Those were duties given me by the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure the interpretation is correct, "Carried out duties." We need to clarify with the witness whether this would be acting Chief of Staff or not, because from what he said in Serbian, it doesn't sound exactly the way it was interpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's beyond the scope of proper intervention, but will you ask the question again, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was: When Dr. Karadzic asked you about your military background today, you also didn't mention to him your position as Chief of Staff when you gave your answer; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm saying I was not pursuing any career there, nor did Mr. Karadzic ask me that question. Second, I was in that chain of command completely uninteresting to President Karadzic at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I do not understand by saying pursuing your career there, but when I asked -- asked you about your specific position at the SRK, you didn't mention that you were -- you were serving as Chief of Staff in 3rd Sarajevo Brigade, did you? Probably you said that you were sent out in the -- in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My main duties were at the corps command, and they would send me sometimes to Vogosca and to Ilidza and to Blazuj and Hadzici to lend assistance. I thought it was an auxiliary duty just to support the personnel that was in command of those areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So did you or did you not take the position of the Chief of Staff in the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade, as Mr. Beara referred to in this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was there for about a month and a half, perhaps two months, as Chief of Staff until the real command was established staffed with commanding officers of the land forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go back to this document again briefly, 65 ter 248073. Now, this document indicates that the briefing that Colonel Beara had was also attended by Jovo Ostojic, and in this briefing -- or pardon me, before the briefing Colonel Beara said you had a talk with him and you told him that Ostojic had confronted you for not giving the volunteers any uniforms, weapons, or other equipment, and so you gave them what they asked for. You gave the volunteers the arms they asked for. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: They did not have weapons. They came without weapons and asked for them because they were not able to go up there. I did not give them. They found them somehow, and then they got duties, but I don't remember this Ljubisa or contacting him in Vogosca at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Colonel Beara reports at the last line of the second paragraph on this page: "Maksimovic rose above the whole thing and ordered his logistics assistant to equip the volunteer unit." So they may have entered the theatre unarmed, but the arms came at your direction, Mr. Maksimovic, didn't they?
