utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not make that decision to arm them. Somebody above me made that decision and ordered it, because I did not have those competencies and did not command the depots. They returned the weapons when they were going back, leaving us 25 days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, if -- who then was the somebody above you who issued the order to equip the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: That happened somehow spontaneously, because we had this crisis towards Vis. Weapons were gathered and given them. The logistics armed them. They listed them all and they sent them to positions. We were not happy, and 25 days later we pulled them back, disarmed them, and sent them home.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that arms were released from SRK weapons stores to volunteers on a spontaneous basis, spontaneously?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: The SRK had nothing to do with it. Weapons were gathered from the Vogosca brigade, from the Ilijas Brigade. There was a surplus weapon there. Those weapons were taken and distributed to them. The SRK had no weapons stores.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your evidence, because you've just said the SRK had nothing to do with it and weapons were gathered from the Vogosca and Ilijas Brigades. Were they not SRK brigade units?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were part of the SRK, but they have their own logistics organs. The SRK can't meddle in those details. So things were gathered from the Vogosca and Ilijas Brigade, from deceased soldiers, because we had difficulty in obtaining this materiel. We gathered some items, gave them to them and they went to positions. While they were there, they weren't very disciplined. We sent them back and took the weapons from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's look at this document a little bit more, and I want to go over to page 3 in the English, the top of page 3, and to scroll right down to the bottom of page 2. Now, this -- you've said in your statement that the numbers of unarmed volunteers, which we now know are Vojvoda Jovo Ostojic's group, the numbers -- their number was 40. Now, Colonel Beara writes that on 26 March, 95 volunteers came to the brigade and another seven on 11 April, which is more than two times the number of volunteers you indicated in the statement you signed for Dr. Karadzic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I gave an accurate document. I don't know where Beara got this figure from. He probably knew more, but they didn't come to where we were. He was a high-ranking officer. I stand by what I say. The figure of 40 is correct. As for his data, I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that Colonel Beara knew more about this than you did?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: He certainly did. He was -- well ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you like to finish your sentence?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I said he certainly knew more than I did. He was a member of the Main Staff. He had records. He had an insight into the entire Army of Republika Srpska, so I can't compare myself to him with regard to the information he had about the army and with regard to who had what.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this admitted as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24073 receives number P6054, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you referred to a document with a 65 ter number 1D08110. It was a SRK combat report of 19 June 1994, and if we can have a look at that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I believe the full translation has now been uploaded, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And go over to, I think, paragraph 9 of this report. Uh-huh. Section 9. And now if we could go over to subparagraph (d), please, in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, subparagraph (d), 9(d) of this document, Mr. Maksimovic, recommends to the VRS Main Staff that: "Naval captain Radomir Maksimovic should be urgently relieved of his duty as Chief of Staff in the 3rd Infantry Brigade and deployed outside the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps according to the decision of the VRS Main Staff because he has a negative effect on his surroundings."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. To go on to another area, and it's about arming, I'd like to call up 65 ter 11199, please. It's an interview with "Nin" by General Kukanjac, and the interview you can see in front of you is entitled "My Truth," and it was given in Belgrade on 6 January 2000. It's a kind of a report by General Kukanjac about the events in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if we go over to B/C/S page 3, English page 5, I'd like to draw your attention to a particular paragraph. Subparagraph (d) of this page reads according to General Kukanjac: "When we realised what was being done and what was going to happen, we began to pull out the entire mobile assets of the JNA in a timely manner. In an endeavour by both officers and soldiers employing perfect organisation, we managed to pull out, preserve and retain everything. Even if there had been cases of seizure by the enemy, we would immediately make it up manifoldly. The Muslim-Croat horde never got hold of a single plane, helicopter, tank, armoured personnel carrier, gun, mortar, motor vehicle." Now, this is actually quite contrary, I put it to you, Mr. Maksimovic, to what you say in paragraph 66 of your statement, which is that: "JNA weapons stayed in the Viktor Bubanj, Marsal Tito, 2nd military district command and Jusuf Dzonlic Barracks," isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I have seen this interview. I think Kukanjac was already deceased at the time. This is the first time I have seen this, that I have seen these details. And my statement was based on officers who had left the barracks. That was in June. It was based on conversations with them. They said that they had left a lot of infantry weapons there, some sort of a self-propelled rocket launcher, but it has nothing to do with this text of Kukanjac's. I didn't know Kukanjac very well. I'd only known him for a few days. These statements from former JNA officers who withdrew from Sarajevo that I'm referring to -- and he said that they had remained there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please know or be told which period Mr. Kukanjac is speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the witness said he didn't know anything about this. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in signing your final statement, you made an addition to paragraph 33 referring to Muslim offensive operations on 30 May 1993. Can you confirm, Mr. Maksimovic, something you've previously said, which was that this attack on your headquarters was to draw attention to other things while BiH forces could cut the road from Lukavica to Pale on Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. And it was cut off at the time. They cut off the road at one point in time and then got it back, but the command was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And can you also confirm that in response to this, SRK forces launched a counter-attack and returned the BiH forces to their starting positions?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: You know, when it was cut off this was in part of Trebevic which was a mountainous forested area. There was no counter-offensive. The Muslims withdrew after we had returned to our starting positions. There was nothing fierce there. They broke through. We drove them back, and all of this took place in an area of about one square kilometre. Because that road, the Lukavica-Pale road, was of vital importance for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go on to another document from around that same time, 65 ter 07660. It's dated 28 May 1993, and it's from the VRS sector for morale, religious and legal affairs. And it's a report, and I'm quite happy if we could just flip through a couple of pages for Mr. Maksimovic to see it refers on page 1 to Muslim propaganda. And then if we could go over to the next page, please. You'll see in your language at the bottom of the page it refers to Croatian propaganda, and that would be in the subsequent page in English. And is this, in your function as morale and information officer, the sort of document you received from your superiors in the morale and legal affairs sector?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I have seen this document. It's quite possible that high military organs sent this document to us for our information, so that we could be aware of the fact that certain things were being done in the area of propaganda against us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember ever having had this document in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But let's go back, then, to page 1 so you can have a look at it, and perhaps I can ask you this: Even though you might not have had the document in your hands, is this similar to the information you received from your superiors during the context of your work in the morale and legal affairs sector?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to ask this again. Which staff is concerned? We can only see that it's the morale sector, but which level are we dealing with? The witness -- I'd just like to see what period is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we show the last page to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's see to what unit it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And this was sent to the VRS Main Staff, the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, the East Bosnia Corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the Drina Corps, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Does this bear the date at all, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Top left-hand corner of the first page, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes. It's 28th of May, 1993. Yes. Let's continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we still can't see which staff is concerned, which level is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's for the witness to answer whether he knows or not. We are not feeding the answer to the witness. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So my question about this was before we begin this --

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, at the top it says the media for the SR Yugoslavia, the sector for morale and religious issues.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is mumbling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps such reports were sent because all the corps had to be aware of what was going on through the territory of Republika Srpska. So that is quite customary.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Maksimovic, can I just interrupt you again. Perhaps we -- I'd like to point out what might be a mistake in the interpretation. You've just said at the top of this document it says "Media for the SR Yugoslavia." That's not correct, is it? I just want to check that the interpreters trying to keep up with you at speed have been able to hear this properly.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: There's a certain technology, a certain way in which reports are written, you know, when you have two states that are at war with each other, and then you report to your side and what the enemy is doing, and they inform their people about what their enemy is doing. So these reports are quite customary, the reports that speak about propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question before we began this, and I note you haven't addressed the correction in the interpretation, my question when we first began this is -- was: Is this information consistent with the information you would have received in your function as morale and legal affairs officer? It reports on Muslim propaganda, and it lists wartime events throughout the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could go over to the second page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: From Gorazde, from Rudo, from Konjic, and at the bottom of page 2 in English, from Sarajevo. Is this similar to information you received from your superiors, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember such a report. I'm not familiar with this. I received things from the assistant commander for morale and perhaps from Galic, but nothing like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So if we can just look at the bottom of page 2 in English, and it's on the successive page in B/C/S, this reports on 28 May 1993 that: "In the course of the day Sarajevo has once again been a target of heavy artillery shelling by the aggressor. The situation is especially difficult in Novi Grad, city centre and Novo Sarajevo. A woman was killed in Kovaci while two children were severely wounded. Sirokaca, Gadzin Han and Dobrinja were shelled occasionally. Snipers are targeting crossroads of Novo Sarajevo. The clashes which commenced yesterday on Trebevic are still ongoing." Is this what you considered to be propaganda, Mr. Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: This is pure propaganda, pure propaganda, and lies.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you didn't do anything about it, did you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: No. What I have read out here, it's just lies. Truth is the first casualty in war.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you didn't do anything about it, did you?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: There was nothing for me to do. I wasn't aware of the possibility of operating in this way and that we were such savages to act in this way. There was nothing for me to do. I wasn't competent. I didn't receive this. But this is unadulterated propaganda. This has nothing to do with anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Can we go over to page 3 of this document, please, in English. Your indulgence for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, the last paragraph of page 3, above the heading "Croatian propaganda," says: "The General Assembly will discuss today the issues of election of the judges and finances for the war crimes Tribunal which was established several days ago." Is that propaganda?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is or correct information. This can't be linked with what was previously stated in the text. What is correct and what everyone can be aware of is correct, so that's the conclusion I draw. No one can play propaganda issues in relation to something like a General Assembly. So this is all correct, but the other things aren't correct. The movement of tanks and so on and so forth, I don't know where all these tanks came from. I'm not aware of this text that has to do with Muslim propaganda but as for the General Assembly, well, this is a well-known thing. That is what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What differentiates between the two? Why do you call the one lies and the other one not?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is international information from international institutions. It cannot be manipulated. But everything else in the text above is propaganda, the purpose of which is to boost one's morale and to undermine enemy morale, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, just for one last item, Mr. Maksimovic, I'd actually like to play a video-clip when you talk about international information. It's a report from BBC war correspondent Jeremy Bowen, dated 30 May 1993, and I hope my colleagues in the booth have received transcripts so that they can provide you with interpretation. And this report, Mr. Maksimovic, is on -- relating to events in Sarajevo. And I forgot to provide the 65 ter number for the record. It's 65 ter number 40349P.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: "The fighting started at dawn. Sarajevo was woken by heavy artillery, tank fire, mortars, and machine-guns. Is it has gone on all day. "Serb guns have been pounding the centre of the city. The people were warned by local radio to keep off the streets. That has reduced the number of civilian casualties. But everyone is a target in this war and Sarajevo's main hospitals are full. "It is because the Serbs are on the counter-attack. Bosnian government forces have since Friday been advancing up the mountain called Trebevic which dominates Sarajevo. They want to drive a wedge between two major concentrations of Bosnian Serb soldiers. If they succeed, it will be a major victory. But the government's 10th Mountain Brigade, which is doing most of the fighting, has been sending dozens of wounded men down the mountain for treatment. "The fighting is still going on. Civilians in the city expect more shells. This family, which miraculous escaped without injury when a tank entered their flat this morning, said they always expect the Serbs to make them suffer when the Bosnian Army is on the offensive."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have you heard the interpretation, Mr. Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I heard the interpretation, but I can't comment on this because I always have doubts about these reporters, because on the whole they were in Sarajevo. You know, they reported from Sarajevo. So if you'd like to know more about it, George Miller [as interpreted] wrote an "Unholy Terror," and he showed what the propaganda was from Sarajevo that was sent throughout the world, with all due respect for the victims, but I can't comment on this from the BBC.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, this is information from an international war correspondent, Mr. Maksimovic, and you've just said international information from international institutions can't be manipulated. How is this different?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. A war correspondent, well, anyone can be a war correspondent if an agency sends him in. He has nothing to do with institutions, so I'd like to make that restriction. The UN is one thing and the war report is another thing -- if he's in Sarajevo or anywhere else. I doubt the veracity of such reports and George Schindler in his book wrote about propaganda in 2007 and showed the amount of propaganda that was concerned. Although I am sorry for all the victims, if there were any victims, I do have doubts about such reports. War correspondent isn't an authority of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And your evidence in closing based on what you've just said is that you're actually disputing whether or not there were any victims to the shelling and sniping of civilians in Bosnian-held Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not disputing that, but I have certain doubts when I tell you that on the 4th of July in Vogosca we had eight men killed, nine wounded, nine seriously wounded and 23 men wounded, well, no one found out about this in the world. So I have certain doubts about the veracity. There were victims, yes, collateral damage and so on and so forth, but I can't believe that everything this person says is correct. That there was fighting on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: And, madam, there's something else I would like to add if I may. You know, the positions of Serbs in Sarajevo and of the inhabitants in Sarajevo was the same. Everyone was anxious. Every position in the Sarajevo field held by the Serbs was under Muslim fire. I can tell you exactly where certain shells fell and what happened. No one reported on this. The reports that were made discriminated against us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Maksimovic. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency, two or three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, we're going to start with the latest things that you were asked about just now. On the 30th of May -- was there any fighting on the 30th of May 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: This was a day out of hell for us, because on that 30th of May there was a great deal of uncertainty as to whether we'd survive. This was a question of life and death. If the Muslim forces were to penetrate Sarajevsko Polje where there was 80 thousand to 100 thousand inhabitants that would have been a slaughterhouse. There weren't any reporters there. They were reporting from Sarajevo. It was a very difficult day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please 1D1541 in e-court to see what the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was reporting about that day to the Main Staff. 1D1541. Can you recognise this report in terms of the form that you can see and the way things are done?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This is the customary form of reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at paragraph 1, and can you read it out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. "During the day, the enemy systematically violated the cease-fire by firing from all weapons and artillery pieces at our defence positions."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that there was a cease-fire that was in force?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a cease-fire. And I remember now, I don't remember exactly which date it was, but I remember that Galic called us in. It was during the month of May. And he told us to observe the cease-fire as much as possible in order to strengthen the credibility of our corps, and also he said that he had received orders for you that we should not respond with gunfire, and then people were commenting on this saying the president won't even let us defend ourselves. This really was taken care of. We really made an effort not to have anything happen to civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you read this third part in the area, the third bullet point.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Which part?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: "In the area of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade sector of responsibility the enemy also mounted a strong infantry attack using artillery on defence positions in the Zlatiste area. That was that. The lines have not been removed. The attack was repulsed. During combat activities two of our tanks sustained minor damage and two soldiers were lightly wounded."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please. Where was this Muslim artillery? From where were they firing at Zlatiste?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the area was concerned, they could only move along the streets of Sarajevo and they would have sought shelter behind buildings and they would have fired from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you read the other one?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: "During the day over 200 projectiles of all calibres landed on positions of the Mixed Anti-tank Artillery Regiment with no consequences."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to tell you to read this out very carefully.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: "A total of 19, 82-millimetre mortar shells felt on the defence sector Jagomir 8, Brdo 8, and Radava 3."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You misread the previous one. Does it say 200 or does it say 20?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: It says 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we have the next page, please. The next page, please. The fifth bullet point from the top, the Ilidza Brigade.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Ilijas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. The Ilidza Brigade. Do you see it there?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: "The enemy used provocative infantry and sniper fire in the Ilidza Brigade sector responsibility. The broader Ilidza area was shelled with 2 times 155-millimetre howitzer shells, Doglodi sector. Two 20 times to 82-millimetre mortar shells and six times 120-millimetre shells on the Ilidza neighbourhood. There were no injured persons."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness continued speaking. We didn't get any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic -- just a second. Mr. Maksimovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. You are speaking so fast the interpreters didn't understand your last part of -- the last part of your previous answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After you read out the text, what did you say? Could you repeat that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that with all these mortar shells that were falling in our area, nevertheless there weren't any injured persons. I'm trying to say that our reports were 90 or 95 per cent truthful. If somebody wanted to engage in propaganda, since so many mortar shells fell, somebody could have said there were 20 or 30 casualties. This is a very good report. This is an accurate report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you just read the conclusion, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we have the next page in English, 8, conclusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what the atmosphere was like in the corps, and we managed to stabilise our line, and we managed to repulse them. They created a mini bridgehead there, if you can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you interpret this, what I said here, were compelled to or obliged to?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they had to respond to enemy attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1541 receives number D2671, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today you said that people were upset because the president of the republic called for restraint and was thereby undermining necessary defence. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, did it restrain whenever possible? Did they refrain from responding with their own gunfire?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. It was only when it was ultimately necessary that we responded. Michael Rose after all said that cease-fires were mostly violated by Muslims and their provocation. I can confirm this to you, Mr. President. General Galic sent me to the 1st Romanija Brigade near Lizdek and some delegation was coming to Sarajevo at the time, and I was supposed to caution him telling him that he should strictly observe the cease-fire. As I was sitting with the late Lizdek, he is deceased now, we received reports from the Kresca [phoen] Company. Djordje Lukic was very seriously wounded in the jaw, very serious wounds from a machine-gun, 12.7 millimetres, and then the same day an infantry attack was launched all with the aim of making us respond so that they could say once again that Serbs were attacking Sarajevo. We were provoked, but we did not have the capacity or strength to attack Sarajevo and take it. You could only dream of that. Three to one was the principle that they observed. Their soldiers rested for three days and then were held positions on one day, whereas our people were on the front line all the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not catch the numbers involved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe 1.000 people could have been, well, in the modern sense of the word, ready to engage in modern warfare.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 12.000 is not recorded in the transcript. Can you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: The corps had 22.000 men on paper, but out of that, only 12.000 were operational, as it were. They could be used in this defence war. The rest were involved in logistics and other work that was used by the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These 12.000, were they all oriented towards the city, and how long was the front line for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps on the internal ring?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Twelve thousand is the entire Sarajevo-Romanija Corps on the positions within Sarajevo and in the external ring towards Igman, Pazarici, Kiseljak, Visoko, Breza, Gorazde, and so on. So practically we were sandwiched in there, and our only way out was to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. 1D1540. Could we have that, please. This is the day that precedes the day that we've been looking at so far. You mentioned restraint and criticism of the president because he was asking for restraint. Let us take a look at this now. Is this the 29th of May? Again the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps is sending a report, a regular report, to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have page 2 now. It's page 2 in English as well. It's paragraph 2. Two and 8. No page 2? Could you please read out paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: "Members of the SRK are observing the cease-fire as much as they can. Because of heavy firing on the line of responsibility, the 1st Rpbr has increased reconnaissance and observation. All other units have also received a supplementary order to increase the level of observation and reconnaissance." So this was the usual thing that should be done to prevent a surprise. We could not allow ourselves to be surprised. We could not allow a breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does this mean when it says as much as they could?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: People were strained. They could not rest. They could not sleep, and they could not live a normal life generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 8, please, now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the point of reading out the document? We can read it. You ask questions, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, this conclusion in paragraph 8, does it correspond to your knowledge about restraint on the part of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and cease-fire violations by the 1st Corps of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the report that is being sent to you has to be truthful and authentic, and it is true that all the units of the corps were following the order on cease-fire, but unfortunately the enemy was violating it all the time. You know, where the corps command was at Dobrinja there was gunfire coming in practically every day. We had no interest in violating the cease-fire. That did not suit us at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These reports to the Main Staff, are they strictly confidential? Can we have the first page.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Let's see. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1540 receives number D2672, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked today about your paragraph 66 in relation to barracks and weapons.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you stand by the essence of paragraph 66 in relation to barracks and weapons?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I stand by that, because it was already in Belgrade that I found out from the officers who returned from these barracks that that is what happened there. I think that the last ones went to Belgrade on the 6th of June. When I came to Belgrade, since we all lived in this collective accommodation facility, they told me about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D59, could we have now, please. Could you please tell us, this is a military post and the date is the 11th of May, and the Army of Republika Srpska didn't exist at the time yet.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about these wounded persons? Who were these wounded persons? What does this mean, they took charge of the following wounded persons?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: These are the casualties from the 3rd of May. I know Taso Enes. These were the -- these were the victims of Dobrovoljacka Street. I know that. These were the wounded that we exchanged, and they were transferred to recuperate. They're from Dobrovoljacka, the 2nd and 3rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please take a look at paragraph 2, not to read out all of it. Does paragraph 2 refer to -- I mean, is it consistent with what you said in paragraph 66 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about the weapons of the TO, and I don't know about these conditions. I don't know who negotiated. I was not involved in that. But I can tell you that on the 14th of May sitting alone in a communications centre I listened to this conversation. Muslims allegedly asked for 15.000 rifles in order to liberate those recruits and others from the barracks. I'm not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that some general from Belgrade came with weapons? Some weapons were turned over to them, including the weapons that happened to be in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did anyone from the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia come bringing weapons and was the weaponry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Reformulate it. You can ask him who brought the weapons at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who brought weapons from Belgrade for the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know that. I hear of this for the first time. I didn't know anything when I arrived there. I didn't know anyone. I'm not familiar with who brought the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are these the same barracks that you mentioned in paragraph 66?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those are the barracks in Sarajevo. I only knew about Marsal Tito. I learned about the others when I arrived. Viktor Bubanj, Gavrilo Princip, I don't know what barracks is that. I didn't mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this document admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether we need to admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution disputes that weapons were left behind in the barracks and that Muslims had weapons from that source as this witness confirmed, and this document independently corroborates the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's, with respect, a misstatement of the questions and answers on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What about the admissibility?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I find the document -- actually, if we could see the last page of the document, and I could make an observation about authenticity. Ah. I find the document is authentic, Your Honours, just with the caveat that the witness did not agree that these were all the barracks, that the barracks mentioned in paragraph 2 were all the barracks mentioned in paragraph 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Further, he cannot comment on this, being not familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll not receive this through this witness, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you, Colonel, on page 42, you were asked about the decisions concerning the stopping of convoys, and you confirmed these decisions were made at a higher level. How would decisions be made in case there was fighting along the lines, along the routes of the convoys? Were commanders duty-bound to stop convoys?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly if there was combat convoys would have to be stopped. A convoy could not be let through if it was a force majeure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we -- could we see 65 ter 24073.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's now P6054.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not the one. Or it could be possibly. Could we see the page that we've looked at before. I believe it was page 2 or 3. Page 3, I think, in Serbian and in English. Yes. Could we enlarge it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Colonel, may I ask you, you don't have to read aloud, but begin with "The accused Maksimovic," and read to the end of the paragraph to yourself, and tell me what is it that you rose above as referred to here?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom of that paragraph. The sentence begins with "They accused Maksimovic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say "The accused Maksimovic"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. [In English] "They accused." "They accused."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was the usual accusation. I did not agree so lightly to do what they wanted, and then they said I was a traitor, but I let it pass because I didn't want to sink to the level of those individuals. It was not said to my face, but it was said about me behind my back. Nobody told me so to my face but I learned later about these accusations. I had a completely different approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What accusations were usually levelled at military officers by these right-wing persons?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: They were very negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But on what grounds? What did they accuse them off from the ideological point of view?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: That we are lesser Serbs, that we do not support the national cause because we wanted to act like gentlemen, to abide by conventions. That's the way we were brought up. We were not so ruthless. But I'm not interested in that. They said that we were not nationally aware, not enough at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This issue of volunteers, was it regulated by law?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Volunteers? Those volunteers there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. The recruitment of volunteers. Is a volunteer different from a soldier the moment he joins in under the same command?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about generally, but when they joined us over there, they had to be under our command, and that is why 25 days later when we realised they were unreliable, they were disarmed and sent back. It was already the middle of 1992. As of May or June, a very restrictive approach was taken to volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they deployed in a populated area?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that they were. To the best of my knowledge, those 25 who were there, I never met any one of them again. They were not there until 1993. There were no paramilitaries. If they ever arrived, they would be integrated into regular units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This Mr. Ostojic or his unit, did they perpetrate any crime that we know of?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. In those 25 days, they could not have done anything in Vogosca. I don't know about before, and they never came back later. I don't know. This Ostojic impressed me as a reasonable person. He was radical in ideological terms, but he didn't appear to me as a brigand. He was quite reasonable when he talked to me later. We discussed how to organise their disarming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The 10th Mountain Brigade of the 1st Corps is mentioned here. Do you know by any chance who was the celebrated commander of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's this Caco person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was Musan Topalovic, also known as Caco, from what I heard. He held those positions close to Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was written in the document, and there were BBC reports of some kind.

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: He was very ruthless, this commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you do not wish to move on -- yes, I'd like to hear, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have absolutely no idea what document the 10th Mountain Brigade was mentioned in, but in any case, that was far and away outside of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was heard on the video, but I strike that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Last question. Colonel, were volunteers one thing and paramilitaries another thing? Is it the same thing or was there a distinction?

utterances.speaker: RATOMIR MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: There is a distinction. Volunteers have to be under command, whereas paramilitaries were for a while outside of anyone's control, but they were quickly neutralised. It was mostly in the early days of the war that the paramilitaries were present. They were not invited by anyone, and they were not answerable to anyone. Volunteers are something else entirely, and they were under military command. That's what I know. I never dealt with paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Colonel. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Maksimovic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll rise all together. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 5 past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salipur. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Mr. Salipur, before you start giving your evidence, I would like to draw your attention to a particular Rule here at the Tribunal. Under this Rule, Rule 90(E), you may object to answering a question from the accused, the Prosecution, or the Judges if you believe that your answer will incriminate you. When I say "incriminate," I mean something you say may amount to an admission of your guilt or could provide evidence that you have committed an offence. However, even if you think your answer will incriminate you and you do not wish to answer the question, the Tribunal still may compel you to answer the question, but in such a case, the Tribunal will make sure that your testimony compelled in such a way shall not be used as evidence against -- in other case against you for any offence other than false testimony. Do you understand what I have told you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Salipur.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes. If I may say, I need to make a correction, and I hoped to do it here verbally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will come to that, but please make a pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D6724 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the statement on the screen?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there anything in it you would like to correct? You just mentioned something.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Apart from some trivial errors of typographic nature, I have no particular corrections to make except for one paragraph that is completely missing from the statement, and I believe it is important to the meaning of my entire statement and evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it regards what?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: My evidence is about the organising of civilian government in the pre-war municipality of Novo Sarajevo and the wartime municipality of Serbian Novo Sarajevo. At one point, I can't remember the date, all of a sudden one evening the general secretary of the UN, Kofi Annan came to the Serbian Novo Sarajevo. We received him for informal talks, and I believe this is rather an important matter, because the Secretary-General visited an area where proper authorities had been established according to the constitution and the law, and he had proper representatives to speak to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this reported by the media?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: It must have been, because he's a personality of global importance, and I found out later how he came to visit. He had visited Sarajevo before, and he asked, Where are the Serbs? And the answer he got was that they are only 100 metres away. Then he told his entourage and his hosts in Sarajevo that he would like to visit, if that's possible, and that's how he came. That must have been recorded in all sorts of documents in Sarajevo and in the UN and everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us anything about his comments that he made then, something he said during your encounter, something you believe to be important?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: We talked for about an hour, perhaps. We explained to him briefly the structure of the population before the war in the Novo Sarajevo municipality, how the authorities were established and how it functioned beginning with 1989 when the multi-party system was introduced, how the war broke out, that we were a mono-ethnic municipality with large parts of the municipality completely dominated by the Serbian population, and we told him that the separation line established already in the war was firmly there. Nobody attacked anyone else. They just defended their positions. And we answered his questions. He left very satisfied, and on one occasion after the war when Mr. Sarovic became President of Republika Srpska, he told us he had attended one session of the General Assembly and had met Mr. Kofi Annan who recognised him and remembered that visit to our municipality at Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salipur. Now that is on record. And apart from the typos, does the rest of the statement reflect correctly what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: It does, and I maintain that all of it is true. The statement could have been longer and more detailed, but I don't think it was necessary to add more. I believe it reflects the situation in our municipality both before and during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have before you that statement on paper?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For your information, it is the decision of the Trial Chamber concerning the topics not relevant to the indictment that some parts of the statement are redacted. Do you have your statement in the original, the one you signed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: I have it before me and on the screen I see only page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions today, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: You can ask them all over again. The answers will be the same, although some things were as far back as 20 years ago. As long as I live, I will confirm the same things, as long as my memory serves me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salipur.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, may I tender this statement with some paragraphs redacted as ordered, and may I ask for flexibility regarding three associated exhibits that we did not have when we were making up our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, first of all, I'm somewhat concerned. The witness said that apart from trivial errors of a typographic nature he adopted the statement, and then Dr. Karadzic asked him to confirm that the statement was his evidence apart from the typos. My concern is that we don't exactly know what the typos are. Perhaps either the accused could take the witness through those typos now or the witness could be asked to review the statement overnight just so the Trial Chamber is clear as to what exactly the trivial errors of a typographic nature in fact are. Apart from that, in respect of the associated exhibits which are listed on the notification which we've received, we have no objection to the admission of the associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I find Mr. Gaynor's comment fair enough, so I would like you to go through those typos, after reading out the summary, with the witness, if any.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, your Excellencies. I'll ask the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before doing that, we'll admit the 92 ter statement as well as three associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6724 receives number D2673. Document 1442 receives number D2674. Document 1496 receives number D2675. And document 20621 receives number D2676, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will have one more document to present, but after reading the summary. I would now read in English the summary of the statement of Mr. Zdravko Salipur. [In English] Zdravko Salipur was born on 19th of December, 1948, in Sarajevo. He is highly skilled lathe operator by profession. During his career, he was -- he has worked for several different companies such as Geoinzenjering, Energoinvest, UPI and others. Zdravko Salipur was a member of the Municipal Board of the SDS in Novo Sarajevo. At the beginning of the war, he worked for the Novo Sarajevo municipality as head of the technical service. Zdravko Salipur was aware that the Muslims and Croats in BH had established their own political parties in the first half of the 1990s and that the Serbs establish their own party some time later. Zdravko Salipur was appointed as a member of the Steering Committee and a member of the Municipal Board of the SDS, and after its establishment the SDS began to develop local boards in the local communes. The coalition created in the BH Assembly between all the parties was working well until there was a rift caused by the vote on the decisions on the independence of BH as the Serbs have been -- had been out-voted by the other two constituent peoples. Therefore, the Assembly of the Serbian people in BH was constituted on 24th of October, 1991, and local government organs were created. However, after the outbreak of the war and the formation of the Serbian Republic of BH, a decision was made to freeze the work of the Serbian Democratic Party for one year due to the situation and to organise the defence of the Serbian people. Zdravko Salipur had information about the military organisation and arming of the Muslims and Croats in the area of Novo Sarajevo before the war. He knew that Muslims were arming themselves through members of the police, the MUP, and the SDA. Immediately before the war, Mr. Salipur would see them wearing uniforms and carrying weapons. Mr. Salipur also was aware that Mr. Enver Zornic, known as a serious extremist and criminal, was in charge of the MOS, Muslim Youth Association. Two months before the outbreak of the war, the paramilitary units of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League controlled the TV tower on Hum and dug trenches and made bunkers around the buildings. Serbs were not allowed to enter this area. When the Crisis Staff for the Serbian people was established, it made assessment of the political and security situation. Dr. Karadzic at the meetings before the war -- before the fighting broke out insisted that there would be no war. During the fighting, the Crisis Staff took over all the prerogatives and functions of the Municipal Assemblies when those organisations were unable to meet. These organisations were not a vehicle for the permanent removal of the Muslims and Croats from the area of BH. Commissioners appointed by the government had the task of trying to establish the rule of law in Serbian municipalities. Zdravko Salipur considers there to be justifiable reason for establishing the Serbian Municipal Assemblies because the Muslims and Croats were preparing for war against the Serbs. The Serbs felt that they had to organise themselves to not allow a repeat of history. He was aware that the Muslims and Croats also had Crisis Staffs and paramilitary units such as the MOS, the Green Berets, and the Patriotic League. He was aware that before or during the war paramilitary existed and operated in Novo Sarajevo. However, the authorities organised themselves with considerable help to get the situation under control. It concerns the Serb part of Novo Sarajevo. The Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo was within the legal framework, free and independent of the republican organs of administration and it functioned on the basis of the principles of normal and free communication. Zdravko Salipur states that the War Presidencies were formed because an imminent threat of war had been declared. These Presidencies were operational bodies whose function it was to make decisions when the Municipal Assembly was unable to meet. They were not a vehicle for the persecution and destruction of the Muslim and Croatian people. The task of the commissioners of the War Presidencies was to organise and establish the normal work of the local community. To Zdravko Salipur's knowledge, Novo Sarajevo had no prisons, prisoners, or war camps or collection centres in its territory, nor were there instructions or orders from organs of the Republika Srpska to organise such. As barricades had been erected around Sarajevo, Zdravko Salipur, for safety reasons, stopped attending work. When the situation deteriorated, the Serb population of Gornji Pofalici settlement organised themselves in accordance with the principle of territorial defence and they prepared for a possible attack. They organised night guards and armed themselves with weapons they legally owned. The Muslims and Croats in the area still lived and worked normally, moving freely. At the outbreak of the war, many civilians left the area of their own accord and a number of people who stayed assisted with the distribution of humanitarian aid. Two public soup kitchens existed in Grbavica under Serb control where meals were distributed free of charge and everyone, regardless of ethnicity, received the same treatment. The same principle applied to anyone entitled to a pension. The whole population had complete freedom of movement. However, they were undoubtedly under sniper fire from the Muslim forces, and many people of all ethnicities were killed in this way. Towards the end of the war, people were unable to -- were able to move across different parts of Sarajevo, across the line -- lines with permission and approval by both sides. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Salipur, perhaps you came across some typos in the first version. We haven't found any, but have you found any that you would like to draw our attention to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: The last paragraph, paragraph 31. It says that the president of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo who was killed was Ljubo Obradovic. The mistake is in that the name was Budo Obradovic. That's the man. So there was a typo, or the person who was listening to me did not understand me correctly. Perhaps there are a few letters that are mistaken. In one place it says Bosa was killed. The name should be Rosa. So if you change one letter, the name is changed too. In the paragraph that you read out in relation to Zornic Enver, in my statement I said that I heard that he was an extremist and that in the course of the war he was involved in various activities. I'm not competent to call these activities crimes but I did hear certain things about this. I can't confirm this fully, but the reason is that on one occasion at the beginning of May I was stopped in the federal part of Sarajevo which was under Muslim control. The police stopped me there. When they had a look at my papers, another vehicle, passenger vehicle, stopped by me. Zornic Enver was at the wheel. I knew him well. He was wearing a camouflage uniform, and he had a green beret on his head, and by his side in the passenger seat there was someone I didn't know also in uniform. The policeman who checked my papers approached the car and spoke to Enver Zornic, and after one minute the car left and the policeman returned my papers and very courteously told me that I could leave. My conclusion is that Zornic told him to let me go. At the time if someone accused someone else of being an SDS member, he would be killed immediately, if such a false accusation was made. So this person treated me correctly. So in spite of the rumours that I have heard, I don't want to say anything that I haven't heard about myself. I've just said what the rumours were, and I read about this in the federal media after the war. So that's all I have to say about that. I just wanted to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salipur. That is very fair on your part. The paragraph in which the woman is referred to has been deleted, but we should say that in the penultimate line of paragraph 31, the person concerned is Budo Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are there any other corrections that you need to make?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Not really. In one of the paragraphs, number 7. These documents are mentioned, the Prosecution documents. When the Serbian municipality of Novo Sarajevo was formed on the 27th of March, at the end of that paragraph it says that on that occasion Dr. Milivoje Prijic was selected as the president of the municipality and Branko Radan as the president of the Executive Committee. They weren't elected at that Assembly. It was only an unofficial Assembly. They were elected after the war had broken out, one gathering that was held in Lukavica. So that shouldn't have been contained in that paragraph. It should have been listed elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salipur. Could we see 1D6727. At some point in time did you have a child in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where and when was he born?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: My son, Ratomir, was given that name, Ratomir, because he lived in wartime and we wanted him to grow up in peacetime. On the whole, children who were born at the beginning of the war would often get such names. You remember Dr. Ratomir Golijan, who was born in 1941, and for the very same reasons he has the same name. My son was born on the 20th of April, 1992. All the media, all the propaganda that I heard stated that at the beginning of the war we shelled the maternity ward and destroyed it. I provided you with the original letter of discharge from the maternity ward which shows that -- which shows when my son was born. He is now 21 years old, and he's studying at the university of agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 15, after the 20th of April, 1992, it should say he was born in the maternity ward. Could you tell us where the maternity ward is where he was born, and where is this maternity ward which we apparently destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: This is the town maternity ward at Jezero. It's called Zehira Muhidovic [phoen], something like that. You can find the name in the statement, but I can't find it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it's at Betanija; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's the lake, in fact. There's a children's hospital and a maternity ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did we destroy that maternity ward?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: No, it wasn't destroyed. Since it was between the lines, later the UNPROFOR was there throughout the war, or IFOR. The name changed. But they were there at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this a discharge letter for your son?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes. It's original.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, could I suggest that this document be marked for identification. We have the date of birth, the time, everything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My wife worked in this maternity ward for 14 years before the war broke out, and all the professors from the clinic and everyone else knew her very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it, but we will put it under -- we'll mark it for identification pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D6727 receives number D2677, Your Honours, MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one other thing I'd like to clarify. Given the propaganda that was spread, on the 20th of April, according to the propaganda that was spread, was the maternity ward already destroyed? When your son was born did the media say that it had already been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKO SALIPUR
utterances.text: Yes. From the beginning of the war there was electronic media. You know there was no printed press but the electronic media stated that it was constantly under artillery fire and that wasn't true. As proof I can say that I took my wife to the maternity ward. I left her there and took her out on the third day. All the staff knew me there because she worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salipur.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, at this point in time I have no further questions, but I'm looking at the time. I don't know whether we have time for the next witness. Perhaps it would be better to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. As you have noted, Mr. Salipur -- if my pronunciation is not proper, please accept my apologies. Mr. Salipur, your evidence in chief was admitted in writing in most part in lieu of your oral testimony. You'll be now cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor, but given the time, we'll adjourn for today and continue tomorrow morning. And I would like to advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood that. Thank you.
